title: Time, Speed & Distance (Trains, Boats, Races)
why: The 2022 IPO paper asked at least two direct questions from this chapter: a train overtaking another train and the average speed of a round trip. The same relative-speed idea also comes back in the mechanics questions (the rain-and-umbrella problem). Almost every question fits one of 6–7 fixed patterns, and each takes under a minute once you know them. That makes this one of the cheapest chapters for marks.

lessons.title: Speed, distance and time from zero
lessons.body:
### The one idea behind the whole chapter
If you walk 5 km every hour for 3 hours, you cover $5 \times 3 = 15$ km. The whole chapter is built on that one line:

$$\text{Distance} = \text{Speed} \times \text{Time}$$

Rearrange it when you need something else:

| You want | Formula | Memory trick |
|---|---|---|
| Distance | $D = S \times T$ | multiply |
| Speed | $S = \dfrac{D}{T}$ | "per" means divide: km **per** hour |
| Time | $T = \dfrac{D}{S}$ | how many "speed-chunks" fit into the distance |

Picture a triangle with D on top and S, T at the bottom. Cover the letter you want, and the other two show you whether to multiply or divide.

### Units must match
The formula only works if the units agree: km with hours gives km/h, metres with seconds gives m/s. The exam mixes them on purpose (train length in metres, speed in km/h).

**Converting km/h to m/s.** 1 km = 1000 m and 1 h = 3600 s, so
$$1\ \text{km/h} = \frac{1000}{3600}\ \text{m/s} = \frac{5}{18}\ \text{m/s}$$

- km/h → m/s: multiply by $\frac{5}{18}$ (the number gets **smaller**)
- m/s → km/h: multiply by $\frac{18}{5}$ (the number gets **bigger**)

Learn this table by heart. These pairs come up again and again:

| km/h | 18 | 36 | 54 | 72 | 90 | 108 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| m/s | 5 | 10 | 15 | 20 | 25 | 30 |

**Minutes to hours:** divide by 60. So 4 h 30 min = 4.5 h (**not** 4.3 h), 20 min = $\frac13$ h, 45 min = $\frac34$ h, 12 min = 0.2 h.

### Mini example
A cyclist rides at 18 km/h. How far does he go in 40 seconds?
- Convert: $18 \times \frac{5}{18} = 5$ m/s
- Distance $= 5 \times 40 = 200$ m

### How to recognise it in the exam
Any question with "km/h", "m/s", "how long", "how far" or "at what speed". Your first step is always the same: **write the unit next to each number and convert so they match**, then calculate.

lessons.title: Average speed: the most common trap
lessons.body:
### Intuition
You drive to a town at 30 km/h and come back at 20 km/h. Is your average 25 km/h? **No.** You spend *more time* at the slow speed, so the average is pulled towards 20.

### The only correct definition
$$\text{Average speed} = \frac{\text{Total distance}}{\text{Total time}}$$

Never just average the speeds unless the **times** are equal.

### Shortcuts
| Situation | Average speed |
|---|---|
| **Equal distances** at speeds $x$ and $y$ (round trip, "half the distance") | $\dfrac{2xy}{x+y}$ |
| **Equal times** at speeds $x$ and $y$ ("half the time") | $\dfrac{x+y}{2}$ |
| Three equal distances at $x, y, z$ | $\dfrac{3xyz}{xy+yz+zx}$ |

Why $\frac{2xy}{x+y}$? Call the one-way distance $d$. Total time $= \frac{d}{x} + \frac{d}{y}$. Average $= \frac{2d}{d/x + d/y} = \frac{2xy}{x+y}$. The $d$ cancels, so the actual distance does not matter.

### Mini example
Going at 30 km/h, returning at 20 km/h:
$$\frac{2 \times 30 \times 20}{30+20} = \frac{1200}{50} = 24 \text{ km/h}$$
Check it with a made-up distance of 60 km each way: time = 2 h + 3 h = 5 h, total distance 120 km, average $= 120 \div 5 = 24$. Same answer.

### How to recognise it in the exam
Look for "round trip", "goes and returns", "half the distance at … and the rest at …" or "average speed for the whole journey". Equal distances → $\frac{2xy}{x+y}$. The answer is always **less than** the simple average, so if an option equals $\frac{x+y}{2}$, that option is the trap.

lessons.title: Relative speed: meeting and chasing
lessons.body:
### Intuition
You sit in a train moving at 60 km/h. Another train beside you, going the same way at 50 km/h, seems to crawl backwards at only 10 km/h. A train coming the other way at 50 km/h seems to rush past at 110 km/h. The speed one object "sees" the other moving at is the **relative speed**.

| Movement | Relative speed | Example (60 and 50) |
|---|---|---|
| Same direction | difference $a - b$ | 10 km/h |
| Opposite directions (towards or away) | sum $a + b$ | 110 km/h |

### Two standard uses
**Meeting (moving towards each other):** time to meet $= \dfrac{\text{gap}}{a+b}$.

**Chasing (same direction):** time to catch up $= \dfrac{\text{head start}}{a-b}$.

### Mini example
A thief is 200 m ahead of a policeman. The thief runs at 5 m/s, the policeman at 7 m/s. Time to catch him $= \frac{200}{7-5} = 100$ s. In that time the policeman runs $7 \times 100 = 700$ m and the thief runs $5 \times 100 = 500$ m.

### Meeting-point trick
Two people start at the same time from opposite ends and walk towards each other. Both walk for the **same time**, so the distances they cover are in the ratio of their speeds. With a 280 km gap and speeds 50 : 20 = 5 : 2, they meet $280\times\frac57 = 200$ km from the faster one's start.

### How to recognise it in the exam
Look for "towards each other", "in opposite directions", "overtakes", "catches", "chases" or "after how long will they be … km apart". First decide whether they move in the same direction (subtract the speeds) or opposite directions (add them).

lessons.title: Trains: add the lengths
lessons.body:
### Why trains are special
A car is treated as a point, but a train is long. To "cross" something, the train's **front** keeps moving until its **back** has cleared the object. So the distance covered is more than the object's length.

| Train crosses… | Distance to cover | Speed to use |
|---|---|---|
| a pole, a standing man, a signal post | train's own length $L$ | train's speed |
| a platform, bridge or tunnel of length $P$ | $L + P$ | train's speed |
| a walking man or moving car | $L$ | relative speed |
| another train of length $M$ | $L + M$ | relative speed (add if opposite, subtract if same direction) |

$$\text{Time} = \frac{\text{sum of the lengths involved}}{\text{relative speed}}$$

### Mini example (IPO 2022 type)
A train 150 m long at 25 m/s overtakes a train 100 m long running at 15 m/s in the same direction. How long does it take to pass completely?
- Same direction → relative speed $= 25 - 15 = 10$ m/s
- Distance $= 150 + 100 = 250$ m
- Time $= 250 \div 10 = 25$ s

(The actual IPO 2022 question is worked in the examples below.)

### Finding the length from two crossings
A train crosses a pole in $t_1$ s and a platform of length $P$ in $t_2$ s. The extra time $t_2 - t_1$ is spent covering only the platform. So speed $= \frac{P}{t_2 - t_1}$ and length $=$ speed $\times\, t_1$.

### Two trains of equal length
If both trains have length $L$, the distance is $2L$. Forgetting the factor 2 is a favourite distractor.

### How to recognise it in the exam
The word "train" plus lengths in metres. Checklist: (1) convert km/h to m/s; (2) add up every length involved; (3) use relative speed if both things are moving.

lessons.title: Boats and streams
lessons.body:
### Intuition
A river carries everything along with it. Rowing **with** the current (downstream), the river helps you. Rowing **against** it (upstream), the river pushes you back.

Let $u$ = speed of the boat in still water and $v$ = speed of the stream.

| Direction | Speed |
|---|---|
| Downstream (with current) | $D = u + v$ |
| Upstream (against current) | $U = u - v$ |

To go back from D and U:
$$u = \frac{D + U}{2}, \qquad v = \frac{D - U}{2}$$

Remember the **divide by 2**: stream speed is half the difference, not the whole difference.

### Mini example
A boat goes downstream at 20 km/h and upstream at 12 km/h.
- Boat in still water $= (20+12) \div 2 = 16$ km/h
- Stream $= (20-12) \div 2 = 4$ km/h
- Time to go 60 km down and come back $= \frac{60}{20} + \frac{60}{12} = 3 + 5 = 8$ h

### Round trip on a river
The distances down and up are equal, so the average speed is $\frac{2DU}{D+U}$, which is always less than $u$. A stream never helps a round trip.

### How to recognise it in the exam
Look for "still water", "stream", "current", "downstream", "upstream" or "rows". Swimmers and escalators follow the same idea: an escalator moving with you works like downstream.

lessons.title: Speed ratios, 'late' and 'early' problems
lessons.body:
### Speed and time are inversely proportional
For a **fixed distance**, doubling the speed halves the time. If speeds are in the ratio $a : b$, times are in the ratio $b : a$.

**Fraction-of-usual-speed problems.** If a person walks at $\frac{3}{4}$ of his usual speed, he takes $\frac{4}{3}$ of his usual time. The extra $\frac{1}{3}$ of the usual time is the delay.
- "At $\frac45$ speed he is 15 min late": time becomes $\frac54 T$, extra $\frac14 T = 15 \Rightarrow T = 60$ min.

### Late and early problems
A man is late when he walks at speed $s_1$ and early at speed $s_2$. The difference between the two travel times is the **sum** of the lateness and the earliness (one late, one early), or their **difference** (both late).

$$\frac{D}{s_1} - \frac{D}{s_2} = \text{time difference (in hours)}$$

### Mini example
At 3 km/h a boy is 10 min late; at 4 km/h he is 5 min early. Time difference $= 15$ min $= \frac14$ h.
$$\frac{D}{3} - \frac{D}{4} = \frac{1}{4} \Rightarrow \frac{D}{12} = \frac14 \Rightarrow D = 3 \text{ km}$$

Shortcut: $D = \dfrac{s_1 s_2}{s_2 - s_1} \times \text{time difference} = \frac{12}{1} \times \frac14 = 3$ km.

### How to recognise it in the exam
Look for "late", "early", "usual speed", "usual time" or "$\frac{x}{y}$ of his speed". Convert minutes into hours before you set up the equation.

lessons.title: Circular tracks and races
lessons.body:
### Circular track
Two runners start together from the same point on a circular track of length $L$, at speeds $a > b$.

| Question | Answer |
|---|---|
| First meeting, opposite directions | $\dfrac{L}{a+b}$ |
| First meeting, same direction (faster laps slower) | $\dfrac{L}{a-b}$ |
| First meeting **at the starting point** | LCM of their lap times $\frac{L}{a}$ and $\frac{L}{b}$ |

Why? In the same direction, the faster runner has to gain one full lap ($L$) on the slower one, and he gains at a rate of $a-b$.

### Mini example
Track 600 m. A runs at 8 m/s, B at 5 m/s, same direction.
- First meeting: $600 \div (8-5) = 200$ s
- Lap times: A 75 s, B 120 s. Both are back at the start together after LCM(75, 120) $= 600$ s

### Races
"A beats B by 10 m in a 100 m race" means that when A finishes 100 m, B has run 90 m. So their speeds are in the ratio $100 : 90$.

For three runners, chain the ratios. If A beats B by 20 m (A : B $= 100 : 80$) and B beats C by 10 m (B : C $= 100 : 90$), then while B runs 80 m, C runs $80 \times \frac{90}{100} = 72$ m. So A beats C by $100 - 72 = 28$ m, **not** 30 m.

### How to recognise it in the exam
Look for "circular track", "laps", "meet for the first time", "race", "beats by" or "gives a start of". Tracks → relative speed. Races → ratios.

examples.q: A car travels at 90 km/h. (a) What is its speed in m/s? (b) How far does it go in 12 seconds?
examples.solution:
Step 1: Convert: $90 \times \frac{5}{18} = 5 \times 5 = 25$ m/s.
Step 2: Distance $= 25 \times 12 = 300$ m.
Answer: 25 m/s; 300 m
examples.shortcut: Use the table: 90 km/h = 25 m/s (the multiples of 18 km/h are multiples of 5 m/s).

examples.q:
(IPO 2022 type) A man drives to his office at 60 km/h and returns home along the same road at 40 km/h. His average speed for the whole journey is:
(a) 50 km/h (b) 48 km/h (c) 45 km/h (d) 52 km/h
examples.solution:
Step 1: Let the one-way distance be 120 km (any convenient number; a multiple of 60 and 40).
Step 2: Time going $= 120/60 = 2$ h; time returning $= 120/40 = 3$ h.
Step 3: Average $= \frac{240}{5} = 48$ km/h.
Answer: (b) 48 km/h
examples.shortcut: Equal distances: $\frac{2xy}{x+y} = \frac{2 \times 60 \times 40}{100} = 48$. Option (a) = 50 is the "simple average" trap.

examples.q: A train 250 m long crosses a platform 350 m long in 30 seconds. Find its speed in km/h.
examples.solution:
Step 1: Distance to cover = train + platform $= 250 + 350 = 600$ m.
Step 2: Speed $= 600/30 = 20$ m/s.
Step 3: In km/h: $20 \times \frac{18}{5} = 72$ km/h.
Answer: 72 km/h

examples.q:
(IPO 2022) A train 200 m long running at 30 m/s overtakes another train 300 m long running at 20 m/s in the same direction. How long does it take to pass the other train completely?
(a) 10 s (b) 20 s (c) 50 s (d) 25 s
examples.solution:
Step 1: Same direction → relative speed $= 30 - 20 = 10$ m/s.
Step 2: To pass completely, the faster train covers both lengths: $200 + 300 = 500$ m.
Step 3: Time $= 500/10 = 50$ s.
Answer: (c) 50 s
examples.shortcut: (sum of lengths) ÷ (difference of speeds). Speeds already in m/s, so no conversion.

examples.q: Two trains 150 m and 100 m long run on parallel tracks in opposite directions at 54 km/h and 36 km/h. How long do they take to cross each other?
examples.solution:
Step 1: Opposite directions → relative speed $= 54 + 36 = 90$ km/h.
Step 2: Convert: $90 \times \frac{5}{18} = 25$ m/s.
Step 3: Distance $= 150 + 100 = 250$ m.
Step 4: Time $= 250/25 = 10$ s.
Answer: 10 s
examples.shortcut: Add speeds first, convert once (90 → 25), then divide.

examples.q: A boat goes 15 km/h downstream and 9 km/h upstream. Find the speed of the boat in still water, the speed of the stream, and the time to go 45 km downstream and return.
examples.solution:
Step 1: Boat speed $u = \frac{15 + 9}{2} = 12$ km/h.
Step 2: Stream speed $v = \frac{15 - 9}{2} = 3$ km/h.
Step 3: Time down $= 45/15 = 3$ h; time up $= 45/9 = 5$ h.
Step 4: Total time $= 8$ h.
Answer: 12 km/h, 3 km/h, 8 h

examples.q: Walking at 4 km/h a student reaches school 10 minutes late; walking at 6 km/h he reaches 10 minutes early. How far is the school?
examples.solution:
Step 1: Difference of the two times $= 10 + 10 = 20$ min $= \frac13$ h (one late, one early → add).
Step 2: $\frac{D}{4} - \frac{D}{6} = \frac13$.
Step 3: $\frac{3D - 2D}{12} = \frac13 \Rightarrow \frac{D}{12} = \frac13 \Rightarrow D = 4$ km.
Answer: 4 km

examples.q: A and B run on a circular track of length 1200 m, starting together from the same point in the same direction at 5 m/s and 3 m/s. (a) When do they first meet? (b) When do they first meet at the starting point? (c) When would they first meet if they ran in opposite directions?
examples.solution:
Step 1: Same direction: A must gain one full lap. $t = \frac{1200}{5-3} = 600$ s.
Step 2: Lap times: A: $1200/5 = 240$ s, B: $1200/3 = 400$ s. LCM(240, 400) $= 1200$ s.
Step 3: Opposite directions: $t = \frac{1200}{5+3} = 150$ s.
Answer: (a) 600 s (b) 1200 s = 20 min (c) 150 s

traps: Averaging the speeds: for a round trip at x and y, the average is 2xy/(x+y), not (x+y)/2. The simple average is always offered as a wrong option.
Mixing units: a train length in metres with a speed in km/h. Convert the speed to m/s (×5/18) before dividing.
Converting the wrong way: km/h → m/s makes the number SMALLER (×5/18). If 72 km/h becomes 259.2, you multiplied by 18/5.
Train crossing a platform or another train: add the lengths. Crossing a pole or a standing man: only the train's own length.
Same vs opposite direction: overtaking/chasing → subtract speeds; meeting/crossing an oncoming train → add speeds.
Boats: stream speed = (downstream − upstream)/2. Forgetting the ÷2 gives double the correct answer.
Time notation: 4 h 30 min is 4.5 h, not 4.3 h; 18 min is 0.3 h. Always divide minutes by 60.
Two trains of EQUAL length L: the distance to pass is 2L. Solving for the distance and forgetting to halve it is a standard distractor.

practice.q: The speed 72 km/h expressed in m/s is:
practice.explanation:
To change km/h to m/s, multiply by $\frac{5}{18}$.
$72 \times \frac{5}{18} = 4 \times 5 = 20$ m/s.
Answer: (a) 20 m/s
Shortcut: Table: 18→5, 36→10, 54→15, 72→20.

practice.q: A car covers 360 km in 4 hours 30 minutes. Its speed is:
practice.explanation:
4 h 30 min $= 4 + \frac{30}{60} = 4.5$ h (not 4.3 h).
Speed $= \frac{360}{4.5} = 80$ km/h.
Answer: (b) 80 km/h

practice.q: A train 150 m long passes a telegraph pole in 9 seconds. Its speed in km/h is:
practice.explanation:
Passing a pole: distance = length of train = 150 m.
Speed $= \frac{150}{9} = \frac{50}{3}$ m/s.
In km/h: $\frac{50}{3} \times \frac{18}{5} = 60$ km/h.
Answer: (c) 60 km/h

practice.q: A man walks at 5 km/h. How many minutes will he take to walk 2.5 km?
practice.explanation:
Time $= \frac{D}{S} = \frac{2.5}{5} = 0.5$ h.
$0.5$ h $= 0.5 \times 60 = 30$ minutes.
Answer: (d) 30 minutes

practice.q: The speed of a boat in still water is 10 km/h and the speed of the stream is 2 km/h. How long will the boat take to go 36 km downstream?
practice.explanation:
Downstream speed $= 10 + 2 = 12$ km/h.
Time $= \frac{36}{12} = 3$ h.
Answer: (c) 3 h

practice.q: Two cars start from the same point at the same time and move in opposite directions at 40 km/h and 50 km/h. How far apart are they after 2 hours?
practice.explanation:
Opposite directions → relative speed $= 40 + 50 = 90$ km/h.
Distance apart after 2 h $= 90 \times 2 = 180$ km.
Answer: (a) 180 km

practice.q: A speed of 15 m/s is the same as:
practice.explanation:
m/s to km/h: multiply by $\frac{18}{5}$.
$15 \times \frac{18}{5} = 3 \times 18 = 54$ km/h.
Answer: (b) 54 km/h

practice.q: A bus covers a certain distance in 6 hours at 50 km/h. At what speed must it travel to cover the same distance in 5 hours?
practice.explanation:
Distance $= 50 \times 6 = 300$ km.
New speed $= \frac{300}{5} = 60$ km/h.
Answer: (d) 60 km/h
Shortcut: Speed ∝ 1/time: $50 \times \frac{6}{5} = 60$.

practice.q: A train 180 m long running at 25 m/s overtakes another train 270 m long running at 16 m/s in the same direction. The time taken to pass it completely is:
practice.explanation:
Same direction → relative speed $= 25 - 16 = 9$ m/s.
Distance = sum of lengths $= 180 + 270 = 450$ m.
Time $= \frac{450}{9} = 50$ s.
Answer: (c) 50 s
Shortcut: (sum of lengths)/(difference of speeds).

practice.q: A cyclist rides up a hill at 12 km/h and comes back down the same road at 20 km/h. His average speed for the whole trip is:
practice.explanation:
Up and down the same road → equal distances → average speed $= \frac{2xy}{x+y}$.
$= \frac{2 \times 12 \times 20}{12 + 20} = \frac{480}{32} = 15$ km/h.
Check with a 60 km road: 5 h up + 3 h down = 8 h for 120 km → 15 km/h.
(16 km/h is the simple average, wrong because he spends more time at 12 km/h; 7.5 forgets the 2.)
Answer: (a) 15 km/h

practice.q: A train 240 m long running at 54 km/h crosses a platform in 28 seconds. The length of the platform is:
practice.explanation:
Convert: $54 \times \frac{5}{18} = 15$ m/s.
Distance covered in 28 s $= 15 \times 28 = 420$ m.
That distance is train + platform, so platform $= 420 - 240 = 180$ m.
(420 m forgets to take away the train's own length.)
Answer: (d) 180 m

practice.q: Two trains 150 m and 210 m long are running on parallel tracks in opposite directions at 70 km/h and 38 km/h. In how many seconds will they cross each other?
practice.explanation:
Opposite directions → relative speed $= 70 + 38 = 108$ km/h.
$108 \times \frac{5}{18} = 30$ m/s.
Distance $= 150 + 210 = 360$ m.
Time $= \frac{360}{30} = 12$ s.
(40.5 s comes from subtracting the speeds; 3.33 s from not converting km/h to m/s.)
Answer: (b) 12 s

practice.q: A boat goes downstream at 16 km/h and upstream at 10 km/h. The speed of the stream is:
practice.explanation:
Stream speed $= \frac{D - U}{2} = \frac{16 - 10}{2} = 3$ km/h.
(13 km/h is the boat's speed in still water; 6 km/h forgets to divide by 2.)
Answer: (d) 3 km/h

practice.q: Walking at 4 km/h a man reaches his office 15 minutes late. Walking at 5 km/h he reaches 3 minutes early. The distance to his office is:
practice.explanation:
One late, one early → time difference $= 15 + 3 = 18$ min $= \frac{18}{60} = 0.3$ h.
$\frac{D}{4} - \frac{D}{5} = 0.3$
$\frac{D}{20} = 0.3 \Rightarrow D = 6$ km.
Answer: (b) 6 km
Shortcut: $D = \frac{4 \times 5}{5 - 4} \times 0.3 = 6$ km.

practice.q: A thief is 100 m ahead of a policeman. The thief runs at 8 km/h and the policeman chases him at 10 km/h. How far will the thief have run before he is caught?
practice.explanation:
Relative speed (same direction) $= 10 - 8 = 2$ km/h.
Time to close 100 m $= 0.1$ km: $\frac{0.1}{2} = 0.05$ h.
Thief's distance $= 8 \times 0.05 = 0.4$ km $= 400$ m.
(500 m is the policeman's distance.)
Answer: (a) 400 m
Shortcut: Thief's distance $=$ head start $\times \frac{\text{thief's speed}}{\text{difference of speeds}} = 100 \times \frac{8}{10 - 8} = 400$ m.

practice.q: A person covers three equal distances at 10 km/h, 20 km/h and 60 km/h. His average speed for the whole journey is:
practice.explanation:
Let each distance be 60 km (LCM of 10, 20, 60).
Times: $6 + 3 + 1 = 10$ h.
Average $= \frac{180}{10} = 18$ km/h.
(30 km/h is the simple average, which is wrong.)
Answer: (c) 18 km/h
Shortcut: $\frac{3xyz}{xy+yz+zx} = \frac{3 \cdot 12000}{200+1200+600} = 18$.

practice.q: A train crosses a pole in 12 seconds and a platform 300 m long in 27 seconds. The length of the train is:
practice.explanation:
The extra $27 - 12 = 15$ s is spent covering the 300 m platform.
Speed $= \frac{300}{15} = 20$ m/s.
Length $=$ speed × time to pass the pole $= 20 \times 12 = 240$ m.
Answer: (a) 240 m

practice.q: On a circular track of length 600 m, A and B start from the same point at the same time at 4 m/s and 6 m/s in opposite directions. After how long do they meet for the first time?
practice.explanation:
Opposite directions → together they cover $4 + 6 = 10$ m every second.
They meet when together they have covered one lap: $\frac{600}{10} = 60$ s.
(300 s would be the answer for the same direction.)
Answer: (d) 60 s

practice.q: Two trains start at the same time from stations A and B, 300 km apart, and travel towards each other at 60 km/h and 40 km/h. When they meet, how much farther has the faster train travelled than the slower one?
practice.explanation:
Meeting time $= \frac{300}{60 + 40} = 3$ h.
Faster train: $60 \times 3 = 180$ km; slower: $40 \times 3 = 120$ km.
Difference $= 180 - 120 = 60$ km.
Answer: (b) 60 km
Shortcut: Split 300 in the ratio 3 : 2 → 180 and 120.

practice.q: A boat goes 24 km upstream and 36 km downstream in 6 hours. It goes 36 km upstream and 24 km downstream in 6.5 hours. The speed of the stream is:
practice.explanation:
Let upstream speed = U and downstream speed = D.
$\frac{24}{U} + \frac{36}{D} = 6$ and $\frac{36}{U} + \frac{24}{D} = 6.5$.
Add: $60\left(\frac1U + \frac1D\right) = 12.5 \Rightarrow \frac1U + \frac1D = \frac{5}{24}$.
Subtract: $12\left(\frac1U - \frac1D\right) = 0.5 \Rightarrow \frac1U - \frac1D = \frac{1}{24}$.
So $\frac1U = \frac18$ (U = 8) and $\frac1D = \frac1{12}$ (D = 12).
Stream $= \frac{12 - 8}{2} = 2$ km/h. (10 km/h is the boat's speed.)
Answer: (c) 2 km/h
Shortcut: Test options: stream 2, boat 10 → U = 8, D = 12: $3 + 3 = 6$ h ✓ and $4.5 + 2 = 6.5$ h ✓.

practice.q: A train passes a man walking at 3 km/h in the same direction in 10 seconds, and passes another man walking at 6 km/h in the opposite direction in 9 seconds. The speed of the train is:
practice.explanation:
Let the train's speed be $v$ km/h. The length is the same in both cases.
Same direction: $L = (v - 3) \times \frac{5}{18} \times 10$.
Opposite direction: $L = (v + 6) \times \frac{5}{18} \times 9$.
Equate: $10(v - 3) = 9(v + 6) \Rightarrow 10v - 30 = 9v + 54 \Rightarrow v = 84$ km/h.
(Check: $L = 81 \times \frac{5}{18} \times 10 = 225$ m.)
Answer: (d) 84 km/h
Shortcut: Test options: 84 → $81 \times 10 = 810$ and $90 \times 9 = 810$ ✓.

practice.q: A man travels 24 km at 6 km/h, another 24 km at 8 km/h and a further 24 km at 12 km/h. His average speed for the whole journey is:
practice.explanation:
Times: $\frac{24}{6} + \frac{24}{8} + \frac{24}{12} = 4 + 3 + 2 = 9$ h.
Total distance $= 72$ km.
Average $= \frac{72}{9} = 8$ km/h.
(8.67 is the simple average of the speeds, which is wrong.)
Answer: (a) 8 km/h

practice.q: In a 100 m race, A beats B by 10 m and B beats C by 10 m. By how many metres does A beat C in a 100 m race?
practice.explanation:
When A runs 100 m, B runs 90 m.
When B runs 100 m, C runs 90 m, so when B runs 90 m, C runs $90 \times \frac{90}{100} = 81$ m.
So when A finishes 100 m, C has run 81 m.
A beats C by $100 - 81 = 19$ m.
Answer: (b) 19 m
Shortcut: Multiply the fractions: $\frac{9}{10} \times \frac{9}{10} = \frac{81}{100}$.

practice.q: Walking at $\frac{3}{4}$ of his usual speed, a man reaches his office 20 minutes late. His usual time to reach the office is:
practice.explanation:
At $\frac34$ of the speed, time becomes $\frac43$ of the usual time $T$.
Extra time $= \frac43 T - T = \frac13 T = 20$ min.
$T = 60$ minutes.
(80 minutes is the new, slower time.)
Answer: (c) 60 minutes

practice.q: Two trains of equal length are running on parallel lines in the same direction at 46 km/h and 36 km/h. The faster train passes the slower train in 36 seconds. The length of each train is:
practice.explanation:
Relative speed $= 46 - 36 = 10$ km/h $= 10 \times \frac{5}{18} = \frac{25}{9}$ m/s.
Distance covered $= \frac{25}{9} \times 36 = 100$ m.
This distance is both lengths: $2L = 100 \Rightarrow L = 50$ m.
(100 m forgets that there are two trains.)
Answer: (b) 50 m
